messages.subject: Comparing local temperatures from different sources: did I do this right?
messages.subject_clean: Comparing local temperatures from different sources: did I do this right?
messages.body_plain:
Hello folks,

I am currently comparing different sources of temperature data to evaluate how much they capture microclimates.

I have a set of iButtons distributed along hills and mountains in Alberta, Canada, and I am comparing those air temperatures with micro_ncep() and ClimateNA <https://cfcg.forestry.ubc.ca/projects/climate-data/climatebcwna/> (coarser climate) outputs at every location (with lat and longs). To make those temperatures estimates comparable, I had to calculate Tmax for each month from the iButtons and micro_ncep() ouputs (i.e., average daily Tmax for each month). When comparing the three sources I noticed that temperatures from micro_ncep() are consistently lower. ClimateNA tends to overestimate temperature.

Here is an example of a mountain (each line represent a location within that mountain).

I also noticed that the differences in temperatures tend do increase with increasing solar radiation (not shown in here).

Question: Am I missing something from micro_ncep() function?

I basically used the default inputs, except by Refhyt, which I set to 1.5m (i.e., same height in which we set up the iButtons), and then looped for each Lat/Long.

I am using TAREF (temperature at reference height) from 'metout' to compute Tmax and compare with iButtons.

Any thoughts?

Here is my code:

micro<-list()
for(i in 1:nrow(microclima_data)){         #microclima_data countains lats and longs
id<-microclima_data$id[[i]]
loc <- c(microclima_data$Lon[[i]],microclima_data$Lat[[i]]) # (longitude, latitude)
dstart <- "01/07/2014" # start date
dfinish <- "30/07/2016" # end date
DEP <- c(0, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200) # specify depths
save = 0 # save the input data (setting save = 2 uses previously saved input)
micro[[i]]<- micro_ncep(loc = loc, dstart = dstart, dfinish = dfinish, DEP = DEP, save = save,slope=NA,aspect=NA,Refhyt=1.5)
}

Cheers,

Cesar

messages.body_plain:
Hi Cesar,

Welcome to the group.

You should not change 'Refhyt' from 2 m - that is the reference height of the air temperature (and wind speed and humidity) measurements of the source data you are using. 'Usrhyt' is the one you want to change - it is he height you want to estimate at.

How did you set up your iButtons? Were they properly shielded from solar radiation? This article has some advice on the issue of measuring air temperature:

Bramer I., Anderson B. J., Bennie J. et al. (2018) Chapter Three - Advances in Monitoring and Modelling Climate at Ecologically Relevant Scales. In: Advances in Ecological Research (eds D. A. Bohan, A. J. Dumbrell, G. Woodward, & M. Jackson) Next Generation Biomonitoring: Part 1. pp. 101–161 Academic Press. [online]. Available from: http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0065250417300302

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: issue with longwave radiation in micro_ncep under shaded conditions
messages.subject_clean: issue with longwave radiation in micro_ncep under shaded conditions
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I just discovered an issue with the micro_ncep function. By default it was using the downwelling longwave radiation from the NCEP database. This is fine for unshaded conditions but will underestimate longwave radiation when shade is present, especially at night. You will notice that the column for TSKY, the sky temperature, was identical in the metout and shadmet output tables as a result.

The alternative approach used in the other microclimate model functions (micro_global, micro_aust, micro_usa, micro_nz) is to estimate the radiation using formulae embedded in the OSUB.f and DSUB.f subroutines in the microclimate model that compute downwelling longwave as a function of air temperature, humidity, cloud cover and shade level. I've now made the latter approach the default for micro_ncep, in the current version on github, but you can use the NCEP hourly longwave radiation data by setting the micro_ncep input parameter 'IR' to a value of 2.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Consider land cover/land use
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

When modeling the thermoregulation of an ectotherm individual using NichemapR, we need to arbitrary set a shade range. However, as many land-cover/land-use datasets have become available in recent years, is there a way to get the minimum and maximum shade according to those land-cover/land-use datasets? Say, if a grid cell has 70% of forest, we set the shade range as 0%-50%, but if a grid cell has 100% of forest, we set the shade range as 50%-50%?

Any thoughts? Your help would be most appreciated!

Best,

Liang

messages.subject: Re: Consider land cover/land use
messages.body_plain:
Hi Liang,

Good question. It really depends on the species and its movement behaviour in relation to the shade. You can have situations where an animal can be in a small area of shade, say a little grasshopper under the shade cast by a single leaf, in which case it experiences the microclimate of unshaded ground except for the solar radiation. Or, it could be in a forest following a sunspot, in which case it is in the equivalent of a fully shaded environment, but with sun on it (!). And you might have a largely open habitat with clumps of deep shade, but the extent that a species uses the really deep shade depends on its ability to move among the patches - e.g. as Mike Sears and Mike Angilletta and co have nicely shown experimentally. You can play with these different scenarios with how you run the microclimate model and how you run the ectotherm model, and you can potentially modify the microclimate outputs before they go into the ectotherm model.

What organism are you thinking of?

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: micro_USA issue, changing ERR?
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

I hope I have not missed a question that has already addressed this.

In short, I am running through a loop of 80,000+ sites to generate microclimate data.  I have done this with micro_global with no issues before.  I am running into an issue with micro_usa and my new terrain data set where some sites are failing.  Of the first 2000 sites, 12 failed.  When I ran one of these failed sites individually I received this error:

"ERROR: the model crashed - try a different error tolerance (ERR) or a different spacing in DEP"

I then changed the default value of 1.5 to 2 and that one site did work.

To put this in further context because I am using my own terrain data, multiple sites pull from the same climate data (~5 of my sites use 1 of the micro_usa climate points) and one of the sites that worked used the same micro_usa climate point as the 4 that failed.  So the only difference between a point that worked and those that failed was slightly different DEM, slope, aspect, and horizon data. I have attached an example file, with green rows working and yellow failing, climate data were pulled from the coordinates in the last two columns.

My question is,  what are reasonable values to use for ERR?  I did not see any detail beyond what is in the help which just says "Integrator error tolerance for soil temperature calculations". I want to 1) make sure I use a reasonable value, 2) avoid having to rerun a ton of missing sites given I am guessing this could happen a bunch over the course of 80,000 sites if I do not use the most appropriate value.

Any insight would be appreciated, thanks!

Vinny

messages.subject: Re: micro_USA issue, changing ERR?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

I'm quite sure it will be to do with the snow calculations which can sometimes become unstable and need a relaxation of the error tolerance for the solution. The issues are occurring with the higher elevation sites.

Are you running the simulations with and without shade? It might be the shaded simulations are where the trouble is occurring and if you don't need the output of shaded conditions you could see if it helps to set runshade=0.

The error tolerance value won't have a huge effect on the calculations and I've only ever need to adjust it when simulating snow, where it will mostly influence the snow itself.

If you play with the error parameter you'll see that as you increase it the variance goes up in the values, with strongest effects on the near-surface (TALOC, soil surface temp) values. But it doesn't get really extreme until you're over a value of 10. Normally you'd want the ERR value to be around 1.5 to 3.

Here is some code you could modify to run the simulations so that it checks as it goes to see if there has been an issue with the integrator - I needed this for exactly the same issue, running lots of sites with micro_usa:

      ERR <- 1.5
      micro <- micro_usa(ERR = ERR, loc = c(Longitude, Latitude))
      gc()
      while(min(micro$metout[,1])==0 & ERR <= 3){
        cat("model crashed, trying a higher error tolerance \n")
        ERR <- ERR + 0.25
        micro <- micro_usa((ERR = ERR, loc = c(Longitude, Latitude))
        gc()
      }

All the best,
Mike

Hi Dave,

Looks like I may have missed that earlier question back in 2017 - it may have been due to a change in the number of parameter inputs which made that code Conor was using fail as Fortran expects you to pass all the inputs and the one from the paper would have become outdated.

Your problem, however, appears to be related to the GADS program (the rungads call). It appears not to have compiled properly. Did you install it via install_github? First try running

micro <- micro_global(loc=c(142,-35), run.gads = 0)

That will switch off the gads program.

Then, if that seems to fix it, and you didn't install via install_github, try that (as explained at https://mrke.github.io/getting_started/).

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: micro_USA issue, changing ERR?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vinny,

Glad to hear 2.5 fixes the issue for you. Out of curiosity, why do you need 0 cm and not, e.g. just a bit deeper in the ground or just above the surface? Be aware that I'm not sure how well the snow model captures what happens in the shade in that there are interception effects of trees on snow. I've put a parameter in there called 'intercept' which cuts down the precipitation that would fall as snow as a simple fraction which you can play with but I've never tried to test it against observations.

Re where to put the code, you could put it in the micro_usa function but perhaps it's better to keep it out of there so that it's easier for you to share your scripts in a reproducible manner.

And re soilgrids, yes I suspect you're getting in trouble with lots of queries to the data.To get around it you'd have to download them which would certainly speed things up - you can do the same with the gridMET data.

All the best,
Mike
